claim: Oh et al. (2014) recently published the most complete description of the mouse mesoscale connectome acquired to date.
source: Oh et al. (2014) recently published the most complete description of the mouse mesoscale connectome acquired to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oh et al. (2014), indicating it is based on prior published work.

claim: The model captures essential principles governing network organization at the mesoscale level in the mouse brain.
source: We show that this model captures essential principles governing network organization at the mesoscale level in the mouse brain
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and analyses presented throughout the manuscript showing model fits to connectome properties.

claim: The model is consistent with biologically plausible developmental processes.
source: is consistent with biologically plausible developmental processes.
evidence: This is supported by the discussion of neurotrophins and developmental mechanisms in the manuscript.

claim: The Allen Institute for Brain Science constructed a mesoscale connectome for the mouse (the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas).
source: The Allen Institute for Brain Science recently constructed a mesoscale connectome for the mouse (the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas), which was the first complete connectivity dataset of a mammalian brain at the mesoscale (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al. (2014).

claim: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas was the first complete connectivity dataset of a mammalian brain at the mesoscale.
source: which was the first complete connectivity dataset of a mammalian brain at the mesoscale (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al. (2014).

claim: Oh et al. (2014) used injections of an anterograde fluorescent viral tracer and serial two-photon microscopy to map axonal tracts.
source: Using injections of an anterograde fluorescent viral tracer and serial two-photon microscopy, Oh et al. (2014) comprehensively mapped both intra- and interhemispheric axonal tracts
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al. (2014).

claim: Oh et al. (2014) estimated the directed connectivity structure among 213 non-overlapping anatomical regions.
source: estimated the directed connectivity structure among 213 non-overlapping anatomical regions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al. (2014) in the preceding sentence.

claim: Basic network properties of the mouse connectome could not be explained by any one standard network model.
source: The authors also conducted a preliminary graph theoretic analysis and showed that basic network properties of the mouse connectome could not be explained by any one standard network model (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al. (2014).

claim: Rubinov et al. (2015) identified small-worldness in the mouse connectome.
source: Rubinov et al. (2015) extended this analysis by identifying small-worldness, a hierarchical modular structure, and non-optimal wiring in the connectome (Rubinov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rubinov et al. (2015).

claim: Rubinov et al. (2015) identified a hierarchical modular structure in the mouse connectome.
source: Rubinov et al. (2015) extended this analysis by identifying small-worldness, a hierarchical modular structure, and non-optimal wiring in the connectome (Rubinov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rubinov et al. (2015).

claim: Rubinov et al. (2015) identified non-optimal wiring in the mouse connectome.
source: Rubinov et al. (2015) extended this analysis by identifying small-worldness, a hierarchical modular structure, and non-optimal wiring in the connectome (Rubinov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rubinov et al. (2015).

claim: Small-world networks are characterized by high clustering among nodes combined with short average path lengths between node pairs.
source: small-worldness (high clustering among nodes combined with short average path lengths between node pairs)
evidence: This is a definition of small-worldness based on established knowledge in network science.

claim: Scale-freeness is defined by power-law degree distributions.
source: scale-freeness (defined by power-law degree distributions)
evidence: This is a definition of scale-freeness based on established knowledge in network science.

claim: Standard small-world and scale-free models ignore directionality, discarding information about differences in incoming and outgoing connection patterns.
source: Second, small-world and scale-free models ignore directionality, intrinsically discarding information about differences in incoming and outgoing connection patterns.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of how these standard models are constructed.

claim: Directionality and spatial embedding are crucial considerations when modeling the brain.
source: Both properties are crucial considerations when modeling the brain (Laughlin and Sejnowski, 2003; Song et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2009; Ercsey-Ravasz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent work in developing plausible generative network models for the brain has primarily addressed spatial embedding.
source: Recent work in developing plausible generative network models for the brain has primarily addressed spatial embedding (Song et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2009; Ercsey-Ravasz et al., 2013; Klimm et al., 2014; Kaiser and Hilgetag, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A common theme in spatially embedded network models is that a node is more likely to connect to nearby nodes than distal ones.
source: a common theme is that a node is more likely to connect to nearby nodes than distal ones.
evidence: This is based on the cited literature on spatially embedded models.

claim: Spatial proximity organizational principle has been able to capture the distribution of connection lengths.
source: This organizational principle has been able to capture a range of properties observed in the cortex, including the distribution of connection lengths (Song et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2009; Ercsey-Ravasz et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Spatial proximity organizational principle has been able to capture the inverse relationship between degree and clustering coefficient.
source: the inverse relationship between degree and clustering coefficient (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Song et al., 2014; Betzel et al., 2015; Mitra, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Spatial proximity organizational principle has been able to capture the relative frequency of three-node motifs.
source: and the relative frequency of three-node motifs (Ercsey-Ravasz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Betzel et al. (2015) reported that individual human macroscale connectomes are well-fitted by generative network models using both spatial proximity and homophilic attraction.
source: Similarly, Betzel et al., (2015), recently reported that individual human macroscale connectomes are well-fitted by generative network models, which use both spatial proximity and homophilic attraction (i.e. nodes with similar graph theoretic properties are more likely to form connections).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Betzel et al. (2015).

claim: The homophilic rules employed by Betzel et al. do not lend themselves to straightforward biophysical interpretations.
source: However, the homophilic rules employed by Betzel et al. also do not lend themselves to straightforward biophysical interpretations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the homophilic rules.

claim: The difficulty of developing biophysically interpretable rules is a recurring challenge in generative network models.
source: Indeed, the difficulty of developing biophysically interpretable rules is a recurring challenge in generative network models (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Song et al., 2014; Klimm et al., 2014; Betzel et al., 2015; Vértes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The authors used the linear model from Oh et al. (2014) to build an adjacency matrix containing connections between 213 symmetric pairs of nodes (426 total) and 8820 directed edges (7804 undirected).
source: We used the linear model from Oh et al. (2014) to build an adjacency matrix containing connections between 213 symmetric pairs of nodes (426 total) and 8820 directed edges (7804 undirected).
evidence: This describes the data processing method used in the study.

claim: The mouse connectome is characterized by a degree distribution with many low-degree nodes and a long tail of high-degree nodes.
source: The mouse connectome is characterized by a degree distribution with many low-degree nodes and a long tail of high-degree nodes (Figure 1a; (Oh et al., 2014)).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1a and citation to Oh et al. (2014).

claim: The degree distribution of the mouse connectome was not well replicated by any standard graph.
source: The degree distribution was not well replicated by any standard graph (Figure 1a and b)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1a and b showing comparisons.

claim: The clustering coefficient distribution of the mouse connectome was not well replicated by any standard graph.
source: nor was the clustering coefficient distribution ‒ a finding also shown in Oh et al. (2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al. (2014).

claim: In the mouse connectome, nodes with lower degree tend to be more clustered.
source: In the connectome, nodes with lower degree tend to be more clustered.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The purely geometric PA model exhibited relatively narrow Gaussian-like degree distributions across several values of L.
source: Relative to the connectome, the purely geometric model exhibited relatively narrow Gaussian-like degree distributions across several values of L (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2a showing model results.

claim: The PA rule fails to generate low- and high-degree nodes.
source: Thus, the PA rule fails to generate low- and high-degree nodes.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The geometric PA model exhibits an inverse relationship between degree and clustering.
source: This geometric model does, however, exhibit an inverse relationship between degree and clustering (Figure 2b) as in the connectome.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2b showing model results.

claim: There is no value of L for which the PA model adequately captures the joint degree-clustering distribution seen in the connectome.
source: However, Figure 2b demonstrates that there is no value of L for which this model adequately captures the joint degree-clustering distribution seen in the connectome
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2b showing model results across different L values.

claim: The purely geometric rules explored in previous studies are not sufficient to recreate the mouse connectome's properties.
source: This suggests that the purely geometric rules explored in previous studies (Song et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2009; Ercsey-Ravasz et al., 2013; Kaiser and Hilgetag, 2004) are not sufficient to recreate the mouse connectome's properties.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results and comparison to prior work.

claim: In the mouse connectome, the in-degree is approximately normally distributed.
source: while the in-degree of the network was approximately normally distributed
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In the mouse connectome, the out-degree distribution exhibited a peak near zero and a long tail, much like an exponential distribution.
source: the out-degree distribution exhibited a peak near zero and a long tail (Figure 3a), much like an exponential distribution.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There was no significant correlation between in- and out-degree in the mouse connectome (ρ = 0.127, p = 0.065, Spearman rank correlation).
source: There was no significant correlation between in- and out-degree (ρ = 0.127, p = 0.065, Spearman rank correlation).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the connectome data.

claim: As the total degree of a node increases in the mouse connectome, the proportion of incoming edges decreases.
source: As the total degree of a node increases, the proportion of incoming edges decreases.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The SGPA model exhibits an in-degree distribution that is approximately normal and an out-degree distribution that is approximately exponential.
source: The SGPA model exhibits an in-degree distribution that is approximately normal and an out-degree distribution that is approximately exponential (Figure 5a, cyan).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5a showing model results.

claim: The SGPA model's degree distributions match the mouse connectome but are exactly opposite for the TAPA model.
source: This is matches the mouse connectome (Figure 3a) but is exactly opposite for the TAPA model (Figure 5a, red).
evidence: This is supported by comparing Figure 5a to Figure 3a.

claim: In the SGPA model, high-degree nodes tend to have a large proportion of outgoing connections.
source: In the SGPA model (and the mouse connectome; Figure 3b), high-degree nodes tend to have a large proportion of outgoing connections.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5b showing model results.

claim: The directed graph theoretic properties of the mouse connectome are best captured by a SG model of network generation.
source: These results suggest that the directed graph theoretic properties of the mouse connectome are best captured by a SG model of network generation.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of SGPA and TAPA models to the connectome.

claim: The mouse connectome has a reciprocity coefficient of 0.13.
source: We found that the mouse connectome has a reciprocity coefficient of 0.13
evidence: This is based on calculation from the connectome data.

claim: The reciprocity coefficient of the mouse connectome (0.13) is high compared to that expected from chance (0.03).
source: which is high compared to that expected from chance (0.03).
evidence: This is based on comparison to a random model.

claim: Reciprocal edges in the mouse connectome are on average shorter than nonreciprocal edges (t(8818) = 13.25, p << 10-10, independent samples t-test; Cohen's d = 0.47).
source: Reciprocal edges in the connectome are on average shorter than nonreciprocal edges (Figure 5c; t(8818) = 13.25, p << 10-10, independent samples t-test; Cohen's d = 0.47).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the connectome data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The reciprocity coefficient of model networks decreases with increasing length constant.
source: As shown in Figure 5e, the reciprocity coefficient of our model networks decreases with increasing length constant
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5e showing model results.

claim: The reciprocity coefficient approximately matches that of the mouse connectome (0.13) when L = 0.725 mm for both the SGPA and TAPA models.
source: approximately matching that of the mouse connectome (0.13) when L = 0.725 mm for both the SGPA and TAPA models.
evidence: This is based on model fitting shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Fitting the length constant to reciprocity in the SGPA model underestimates the physical edge lengths of the connectome.
source: However, fitting the length constant to reciprocity (e.g. in the SGPA model) underestimates the physical edge lengths of the connectome (compare Figure 5c to d).
evidence: This is based on comparison of Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: Incorporating SG into the PA model increases the width of the degree distribution.
source: Incorporating SG into the PA model increases the width of the degree distribution, allowing the model to also capture the joint clustering-degree distribution seen in the connectome (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6a showing model results.

claim: In the connectome, there is a negative correlation between a node's clustering coefficient and its mean edge length (ρ = -0.238, p < 10-6, Spearman rank correlation).
source: In the connectome, there is a negative correlation between a node's clustering coefficient and its mean edge length. That is, nodes with short average edge lengths tend to be highly clustered (ρ = -0.238, p < 10-6, Spearman rank correlation).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the connectome data.

claim: A similar, but stronger relationship between clustering coefficient and mean edge length occurs in the SGPA model (median ρ = -0.482, p < 10-10, Spearman rank correlation).
source: A similar, but stronger relationship occurs in the SGPA model (median ρ = -0.482, p < 10-10, Spearman rank correlation).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the SGPA model results.

claim: There was a close match between the nodal efficiency distributions for the connectome and the SGPA model (with L = 0.725 mm).
source: As shown in Figure 6b, there was a close match between the nodal efficiency distributions for the connectome and the SGPA model (with L = 0.725 mm)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6b showing the comparison.

claim: When nodes were removed in order of decreasing degree (targeted attack), the SGPA model's global efficiency and largest component size both decreased in a manner more similar to the mouse connectome than any standard graph.
source: When nodes (and the edges connected to them) were removed in order of decreasing degree (i.e. targeted attack), the SGPA model's global efficiency (akin to nodal efficiency; see 'Materials and methods') and largest (giant) component size both decreased in a manner more similar to the mouse connectome than any standard graph (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7 showing lesioning results.

claim: The mouse connectome disintegrates the fastest under targeted attack compared to model networks.
source: However, Figure 7a shows that the mouse connectome disintegrates the fastest
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7a showing lesioning results.

claim: The global efficiency falls more rapidly in the connectome than any model under targeted attack.
source: and Figure 7b shows that the global efficiency falls more rapidly in the connectome than any model.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7b showing lesioning results.

claim: The connectome appears more vulnerable to targeted attack than the model networks explored.
source: Thus, the connectome appears more vulnerable to targeted attack than the model networks explored here.
evidence: This is an inference from the lesioning results shown in Figure 7.

claim: In- and out-degree were differentially distributed in the connectome.
source: The fact that in- and out-degree were differentially distributed in the connectome highlights an important limitation of undirected graphs
evidence: This is based on the data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Undirected graphs do not discriminate between in- and out-degree distributions and may fail to reveal key connectivity properties arising from directed structure.
source: they do not discriminate between in- and out-degree distributions and may therefore fail to reveal key connectivity properties arising from such directed structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of undirected graphs.

claim: The C. elegans connectome has nearly identical in- and out-degree (exponential) distributions.
source: For instance, the C. elegans connectome (for the full nervous system) (White, 1985) has nearly identical in- and out-degree (exponential) distributions (Amaral et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White (1985) and Amaral et al. (2000).

claim: High clustering coefficient is thought to indicate potential for participation in specialized computational units.
source: As high clustering coefficient is thought to indicate potential for participation in this sort of computational unit (Rubinov and Sporns, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rubinov and Sporns (2010).

claim: Nodes with a small number of neighbors tend to be highly clustered in the mouse connectome, suggesting they are candidates for specialized processing.
source: our finding that nodes with a small number of neighbors tend to be highly clustered suggests that these nodes are candidates for specialized processing.
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis and established knowledge about clustering.

claim: Connections associated with hub nodes were primarily outgoing in the directed connectome.
source: Surprisingly, connections associated with such hub nodes were primarily outgoing in the directed connectome (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Hubs play a stronger role in distribution, rather than integration, of information in the mouse connectome.
source: Assuming again that anatomical connectivity is indicative of functional relationships, our results suggest that hubs play a stronger role in distribution, rather than integration, of information.
evidence: This is an inference from the data on hub connectivity patterns.

claim: Above-chance reciprocity is hypothesized to be important for functional integration and segregation.
source: Above-chance reciprocity, as we found in the mouse connectome, is also hypothesized to be important for functional integration and segregation (Tononi et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tononi et al. (1994).

claim: Bidirectional connections between brain regions constrain dynamics such that a balance arises between functional integration and segregation.
source: Previous work has suggested that bidirectional connections between brain regions constrain the dynamics in such a way that a balance arises between the two (Tononi et al., 1992; Sporns et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tononi et al. (1992) and Sporns et al. (1991).

claim: If axonal outgrowth occurs in a straight line and the axon attaches to the first node it physically encounters, then the probability of connecting to a target neuron depends exponentially on the target's distance from the source neuron.
source: For example, Kaiser et al. (2009) noted that if axonal outgrowth occurs in a straight line and the axon attaches to the first node it physically encounters, then the probability of connecting to a target neuron depends exponentially on the target's distance from the source neuron (Kaiser et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaiser et al. (2009).

claim: Some chemical gradients responsible for axon guidance decay exponentially with distance.
source: Previous research has also shown that some chemical gradients responsible for axon guidance decay exponentially with distance (Murray, 1993; Isbister et al., 2003) and have been modeled as such (Mortimer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Murray (1993), Isbister et al. (2003), and Mortimer et al. (2009).

claim: Rubinov et al. (2015) reported that distance-dependent inter-areal connection strengths in the mouse connectome were best captured by a power law.
source: Similarly, Rubinov et al. (2015), recently reported that distance-dependent inter-areal connection strengths in the mouse connectome were best captured by a power law.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rubinov et al. (2015).

claim: The purely geometric PA model fails to account for the broad degree distribution of the connectome.
source: We explored a purely geometric model based on PA and found that while this model induces clustering between low-degree nodes, it fails to account for the broad degree distribution of the connectome.
evidence: This is based on the model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only when incorporating the source-growth rule could the authors capture the in- and out-degree distributions of the mouse connectome.
source: Only when incorporating the source-growth rule could we capture the in- and out-degree distributions of the mouse connectome.
evidence: This is based on the model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The in- and out-degree distributions arise independently of the PA rule in the SGPA model.
source: Note that these distributions arise independently of the PA rule, but other characteristics require it, as discussed previously (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for the in- and out-degree distributions of a graph with source-growth but not PA).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing model results without PA.

claim: A SG rule specifically depending on out-degree is a better candidate mechanism for generating the properties of mouse connectome than total degree.
source: This indicates that a SG rule specifically depending on out-degree is a better candidate mechanism for generating the properties of mouse connectome.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing different model variants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Much of the organizational structure of the mouse connectome is captured by the geometric and topological generative rules employed by the SGPA model.
source: Our results indicate that much of the organizational structure of the mouse connectome is captured by the geometric and topological generative rules employed by the SGPA model.
evidence: This is an inference from the comprehensive model results presented.

claim: Brain organization at the mesoscopic scale might not require precise specification of connectivity but might instead be largely based on a set of relatively simple instructions.
source: The ability of these simple rules to closely capture the mouse connectome's network structure raises the possibility that brain organization at the mesoscopic scale does not require precise specification of connectivity (e.g. through genetic or transcriptional factors), but might instead be largely based on a set of relatively simple instructions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the success of the simple model.

claim: Neurotrophins play a major role in promoting the survival of innervating neurons.
source: The source growth rule might be realized during brain development by the actions of a family of proteins known as neurotrophins, which play a major role in promoting the survival of innervating neurons (Huang and Reichardt, 2001; Chao, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang and Reichardt (2001) and Chao (2003).

claim: Neurotrophins play a major role in the growth and branching of axons.
source: and the growth and branching of their axons (Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman (1996).

claim: Neurotrophins are typically secreted by a target (postsynaptic) neuron at functional synapses, endocytosed by a source (presynaptic) neuron, and retrogradely transported to the source neuron's soma.
source: these proteins are typically secreted by a target (postsynaptic) neuron at functional synapses, endocytosed by a source (presynaptic) neuron, and retrogradely transported to the source neuron's soma, where they trigger the above-mentioned processes (Huang and Reichardt, 2001; Korsching, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang and Reichardt (2001) and Korsching (1993).

claim: Neurotrophins are available in limited quantities and are hypothesized to cause competitive interactions among growing neuronal populations.
source: Because neurotrophins are available in limited quantities, they are hypothesized to cause competitive interactions among growing neuronal populations (van Ooyen and Willshaw, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Ooyen and Willshaw (1999).

claim: Populations that maintain many functional outgoing connections will tend to receive more neurotrophins and should on average be more fit for survival and new connection generation.
source: Most importantly, since populations that maintain many functional outgoing connections will tend to receive more neurotrophins, they should on average be more fit for survival and new connection generation, and their existing connections should be more likely to branch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of neurotrophins.

claim: The neurotrophin mechanism would lead to the 'rich-get-richer' phenomenon for outgoing connections that was fundamental in modeling the network properties of the mouse connectome.
source: Such a biological mechanism would lead to the "rich-get-richer" phenomenon for outgoing connections that was fundamental in modeling the network properties of the mouse connectome.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the biological mechanism to the model.

claim: The SGPA model provides an alternative to power-law degree distributions for describing the brain's undirected degree distribution.
source: The SGPA model provides an alternative because the in- and out-degree distributions are driven by different rules.
evidence: This is an inference from the model structure and results.

claim: The distribution over undirected degree is expected to approach the convolution of a Gaussian and an exponential, that is, an exponentially modified Gaussian.
source: Thus, we would expect the distribution over undirected degree (which is approximately the sum of in- and out-degree, the approximation arising since we do not count reciprocal edges twice) to approach the convolution of a Gaussian and an exponential, that is, an exponentially modified Gaussian (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on mathematical reasoning about the combination of distributions.

claim: The SGPA model is able to capture the low-degree portion of the distribution unlike the scale-free graph.
source: Additionally, the SGPA model is able to capture the low-degree portion of the distribution (Figure 1b) unlike the scale-free graph.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1b showing the comparison.

claim: The choice to instantiate all the nodes at the start of the network's generation is somewhat biologically implausible.
source: Our choice to instantiate all the nodes at the start of the network's generation is somewhat biologically implausible.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a model limitation.

claim: A version of the SPGA model in which nodes are added one-by-one yielded a qualitatively similar network.
source: However, a version of our SPGA model in which nodes are added one-by-one (see 'Materials and methods') yielded a qualitatively similar network (see Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the node-by-node SGPA model, the youngest nodes had an extremely low degree and a clustering coefficient of either zero or one.
source: The only notable differences were that the youngest nodes had an extremely low degree and a clustering coefficient of either zero or one
evidence: This is based on analysis of the node-by-node model variant.

claim: In the node-by-node SGPA model, there was a positive correlation between in- and out-degree.
source: and that there was a positive correlation between in- and out-degree.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the node-by-node model variant.

claim: The SGPA model predicts that edge lengths should be significantly shorter than those observed in the connectome.
source: One interesting feature of the SGPA model is that it predicts that edge lengths should be significantly shorter than those observed in the connectome.
evidence: This is based on comparison of model results to connectome data.

claim: The SGPA model is unable to account for both the edge length distribution and the reciprocity of the connectome while also maintaining the appropriate dimensionality.
source: Thus, our model is unable to account for both the edge length distribution and the reciprocity of the connectome while also maintaining the appropriate dimensionality.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a model limitation based on the results.

claim: Within the lesioning analysis, the connectome is more susceptible to targeted attack than the generative SGPA model network (or any other model).
source: Within the lesioning analysis, we found that the connectome is more susceptible to targeted attack than our generative SGPA model network (or any other model).
evidence: This is based on the lesioning results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mouse connectome is less resilient than the synthetic networks explored.
source: This suggests that the mouse connectome is less resilient than the synthetic networks explored here.
evidence: This is an inference from the lesioning results.

claim: Cortico-cortical projections have higher reciprocity than cortico-subcortical ones in macaque macroscale and mouse mesoscale connectomes.
source: A similar point was raised by Kaiser and Varier (2011) and Oh et al. (2014) ‒ both noted that cortico-cortical projections have higher reciprocity than cortico-subcortical ones in macaque macroscale and mouse mesoscale connectomes, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaiser and Varier (2011) and Oh et al. (2014).

claim: To generate a connectivity graph from empirical data, the authors used the mouse connectome developed by the Allen Brain Institute.
source: To generate a connectivity graph from empirical data, we used the mouse connectome developed by the Allen Brain Institute.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: To compile the Allen dataset, anterograde tracers were injected in a single hemisphere and the authors traced projections into both hemispheres.
source: To compile this dataset, anterograde tracers were injected in a single hemisphere and the authors traced projections into both hemispheres.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to generate the data.

claim: The original work computed projection strengths and associated p-values between 213 pairs of ipsi- and contralateral anatomically defined brain regions.
source: The original work computed projection strengths and associated p-values (the probability that the observed projection would arise by chance) between 213 pairs of ipsi- and contralateral anatomically defined brain regions (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oh et al. (2014).

claim: To generate a binary adjacency matrix, the authors set all connection strengths with p<0.01 to one and all other elements to zero.
source: To generate a binary adjacency matrix, we set all connection strengths with p<0.01 to one and all other elements to zero.
evidence: This describes the data processing method used in the study.

claim: The authors assumed that all connectivity projections were bilaterally symmetric in order to construct a 426 x 426 binary adjacency matrix.
source: We then assumed that all connectivity projections were bilaterally symmetric in order to construct a 426 x 426 binary adjacency matrix, which completely defines a (single component) graph.
evidence: This describes the data processing method used in the study.

claim: The results remained qualitatively the same for alternative connection thresholds (p<0.05 and p<0.001).
source: The results remained qualitatively the same for alternative connection thresholds (p<0.05 and p<0.001).
evidence: This describes a robustness check performed in the study.
